name: Aurora Veil

stars.name: Veil Prime
stars.notes: A hot young white star plowing through the dust shore of the Glassward nebula; its ferocious stellar wind strikes the infalling particles and lights every world in the system with permanent aurora.

planets.name: Cinderlight
planets.notes: A scorched rock wrapped in a glowing green haze where the stellar wind grinds against its iron core; beautiful from a distance, lethal at any closer range.

planets.name: Shimmer
planets.notes: An airless world whose regolith glows faintly with charged particle deposition; its night side is never actually night.

planets.name: Lanternfall
planets.notes: A cool terrestrial world under permanent curtains of light: green by day, violet by night. Eighty thousand people live in domed towns built to watch it, and the economy is tourism, wonder, and the science that explains both.

planets.name: Glimmerdeep
planets.notes: A dark ocean world whose seas phosphoresce in answer to the auroras above; charter boats from Lanternfall run the crossing in high season despite the League's frowns.

planets.name: The Pale King
planets.notes: A vast pale-lavender giant crowned by the system's grandest auroral oval, visible from Lanternfall as a ghostly ring on the horizon.

planets.name: Hush
planets.notes: A quiet frozen outpost world at the nebula's inner shore; beyond it, the dust thickens into the Veil proper and visibility drops to nothing.

anomalies.name: The Standing Curtain
anomalies.notes: A filament of glowing plasma that has hung between two orbits for as long as the system has been charted, stable against all models. Ships route around it. Wedding parties from Lanternfall book flybys.

stations.name: Veilside Terminal
stations.notes: The system's port of entry, built like a gallery: long observation halls where arriving passengers get their first sight of Lanternfall's permanent sky before customs says a word.

stations.name: Curtain Watch
stations.notes: A physics platform studying the impossible filament; its staff publish steadily, agree on nothing, and renew their postings anyway.

faction_control.notes: The League administers the system as a protected scenic reserve: development is capped, approach lanes are fixed to preserve the view, and the tourism board's regulations carry actual legal force.

history: The system was charted late because the surrounding nebula dust masked it; the first survey ship emerged from the Veil directly into the auroral glow and its crew refused for three days to believe the light was natural.
Lanternfall was settled by a League cultural cooperative that wrote scenic preservation into the founding charter, making it the first world where the skyline is legally a monument.

Twelve years ago the Standing Curtain brightened tenfold for nine days, bathing every world in violet light; the event drew two million visitors and remains unexplained, which suits the tourism board perfectly.
description: Every sky in this system burns. The young white star's wind meets the nebula's drifting dust and the result is light: green fire over Cinderlight, a glow that never dies on Shimmer's plains, and above Lanternfall the great slow curtains that give the world its name. Even the outer giant wears a crown of cold fire. It is, by consensus of everyone who has seen it, the most beautiful address in charted space.

Eighty thousand people make their living from that beauty. Lanternfall's dome towns host visitors who cross the Veil for the view, scientists who cross it for the physics, and a steady current of pilgrims of no stated faith at all. The League keeps the lanes fixed and the skylines low; traffic is light, seasonal, and unfailingly polite, because nobody wants to be the ship that spoiled the sight.

Two things keep the philosophers employed. The Standing Curtain has hung between orbits for all recorded time, defying every model, and it brightened once, for nine days, as if acknowledging an audience. And the old survey logs record that when the first ship cleared the dust, the auroras across four worlds pulsed in sequence, stern to bow, like a held breath let out. The phenomenon has never recurred. The tourism board calls it folklore. The physicists call it unresolved. Everyone keeps watching.
